newsitem.title: USA: U.S. municipal utilities seek break from tax rule.
newsitem.headline: U.S. municipal utilities seek break from tax rule.

text.p: U.S. public power suppliers Wednesday urged Congress to change a tax law that limits their ability to buy and sell power in the increasingly competitive market.

Owners of public power utilities are limited to earning up to 10 percent or $15 million -- whichever is less -- of their revenue from private users of their facilities. If the limit is exceeded, the bonds become taxable, hitting bondholders and the utilities' customers whose electricity costs increase.

The so-called "private use" rule is holding back public power utilities from participating in new grid operations that call for transmission owners to open their lines to rival power producers to promote market competition.

Public power suppliers "could be handicapped pretty severely if 'private use' is not handled quickly," Clarence Rappleyea, chairman of the New York Power Authority, said at a House energy and power subcommittee hearing.

Panel chairman Rep. Dan Schaefer, R-Colo., who is pushing power market deregulation, last month asked House Ways and Means Committee chairman Bill Archer to address the issue, but has not received a reply yet.

"I commend the issue of outstanding tax-exempt bonds for existing facilities to your attention because it appears that current private use rules for such facilities are a serious impediment for public power in today's electricity industry," Schaefer's June 5 letter to the Texas Republican said.
Electric cooperatives also urged lawmakers to ensure that rural utilities, financed by the federal government, would not not be shielded from competition.

"To deny their members access to open market advantages for the preservation of uneconomic and, in some cases, subsidized generation entities is a violation of trust between the distribution cooperative's membership and its governance, and in some cases will penalize taxpayers," said Gene Argo, president of Midwest Energy, a cooperative that has paid off its debt to the U.S. Rural Utilities Service.

Rural utilities fear that in a competitive market, other utilities will steal their best customers, and in turn the rural suppliers will have to hike rates to their remaining customers who will have little access to other power sources.
